title: A password is in history. Remove it from every commit.
summary: Deleting the file does nothing — the blob stays in every commit that had it. Rewrite the whole history to purge it, then face the part people skip: the credential is already compromised.
mental_model: Removing a file from history means rebuilding every commit that ever contained it. Every sha downstream changes, so this is not a fix you apply quietly — it is a coordinated event for everyone with a clone.
danger: A pushed secret is compromised the moment it is pushed. Rewriting history hides it from future readers; it does not un-leak it. Rotate the credential first, always.

steps.title: Confirm the secret is still readable
steps.why: The file is not in the working tree and not in HEAD. It is still in three commits, and anyone with a clone can read it with a single command.
steps.expect: The password, printed straight out of history.

verify.label: the secret is still in history

steps.title: Rotate the credential first
steps.why: This is the step people skip. Anyone who cloned, any CI cache, any forge's dangling-commit view still has it. Rewriting history is cleanup; rotation is the actual fix. Record it so the history rewrite is not mistaken for a remediation.

write.content:
# Incident: credentials committed to git

- DB_PASSWORD and STRIPE_KEY were committed in config/secrets.env.
- Both rotated before the history rewrite.
- History rewritten afterwards to remove the file from all commits.
- Everyone with a clone must re-clone; old clones still contain the old blob.

steps.title: Find every commit that carries the file
steps.why: Know the blast radius before rewriting. Every one of these commits will get a new sha, and so will everything after them.
steps.expect: Several commits, and the blob still reachable.

steps.title: Rewrite every commit to drop the file
steps.why: `--index-filter` runs against the index rather than a checkout, which makes it dramatically faster than `--tree-filter`. `--ignore-unmatch` stops it failing on commits that never had the file.
steps.expect: Every commit rewritten, and no commit touching the secrets file any more.

verify.label: no commit on any branch contains the file (refs/original still does, for now)

steps.title: Confirm the other config survived
steps.why: A rewrite that also removed app.env would be a disaster of a different kind. Always verify the tree is otherwise identical — this is why you check, rather than trusting the command.

verify.label: the neighbouring config file is untouched

steps.title: Expire the backup refs filter-branch left you
steps.why: filter-branch keeps the original commits under `refs/original/`, so the blob is still reachable and `git log --all` can still find it. Expiring those refs and the reflog, then pruning, is what actually removes the object.
commands: sh -c 'git for-each-ref --format="%(refname)" refs/original | xargs -n 1 git update-ref -d'
steps.expect: 0 — the blob is no longer reachable from anything.

verify.label: the blob is gone from the object database
verify.hint: delete refs/original, expire the reflog, then gc --prune=now

steps.title: Understand what everyone else must now do
steps.why: Every sha changed, so every clone is incompatible. Colleagues must re-clone — a `git pull` would merge the old history straight back in, secret included, which is the most common way this cleanup fails.
steps.expect: A clean history — and a document explaining why everyone needs a fresh clone.

verify.label: no commit anywhere references the secrets file
the blob itself is unreachable and pruned
the rewrite removed only the intended file
the rotation was documented — the rewrite is not the remediation
history is intact apart from the purge

pitfalls: Rotate the credential FIRST. History rewriting is housekeeping; anyone who cloned still has the secret, and so may the forge.
`git filter-repo` is the modern, faster and much safer tool. It is a separate install; filter-branch is used here only because it ships with git.
filter-branch keeps originals in `refs/original/`. Until you delete those and gc, nothing has actually been removed.
After the rewrite, colleagues must re-clone. If anyone merges an old clone back in, the secret returns and so does the whole old history.
On a hosted forge, the old commits may remain accessible by sha until support garbage-collects them. Ask them; do not assume.
